stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department for the third time in the past six months because she is worried she may have colon cancer. Her grandfather died from colon cancer one year ago at the age of 72.In the past year, she has had two normal colonoscopies and a normal upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Routine bloods have all been entirely normal. She is anxious and upset. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Patients with illness anxiety disorder have an unrealistic fear that they have a serious medical condition or fear they are at very high risk of becoming ill. They may misinterpret normal bodily function as indicating underlying illness.This patient has care-seeking illness anxiety disorder, which may have been triggered by the death of her grandfather. Cognitive behavioural therapy is the mainstay of intervention. Q. Answered Flagged o.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with a small-joint polyarthritis which is only partially relieved by regular naproxen. Rheumatoid arthritis is suspected. Which of the following autoantibodies is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies are directed against citrullinated proteins. Proteins become citrullinated during inflammation, which is a feature of active rheumatoid disease. Anti-CCP antibodies can be used to predict disease activity and progression in rheumatoid arthritis. They have a sensitivity of around 74% for rheumatoid arthritis and are more specific for the disease than rheumatoid factor, at around 95%. Q.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to the Neurology Ward with gradually deteriorating consciousness. According to the nursing staff, she has been asleep for most of the day, complaining of a headache when she is awake. She appears confused, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13 when she is awoken. She suffered a subarachnoid haemorrhage some three days earlier and had initially been recovering well. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema. Her temperature is 37℃. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her drowsiness?
explanation: This patient's gradual deterioration in consciousness with a headache and mild confusion is consistent with hydrocephalus after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Symptoms may occur as early as 24 hours after the initial haemorrhage and build slowly over hours to days. A repeat computed tomography scan is the most important next step to confirm the diagnosis. Fourth ventricular outlet obstruction can occur following subarachnoid haemorrhage and is the most likely cause here. Q.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a red, itchy rash affecting both forearms to a level just above the wrist. The skin is blistered, dry and cracked. She works in an animal facility and washes her hands many times per day. She says the rash gets better when she is on holiday. Apart from her current symptoms, examination is unremarkable. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most useful investigation to be performed?
explanation: This patient may be allergic to a range of allergens, either from one of the animal species she is exposed or one of the cleaning products used in the animal facility. With a diagnosis of contact dermatitis and a potential wide range of allergens, patch testing is the most appropriate investigation. ALlergen avoidance is the most appropriate intervention: once a precipitant is identified, the patient could be moved to a new role, be given protective clothing or given alternative cleaning materials. Topical corticosteroids can be used to improve symptoms over the short-term. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Psychiatry Clinic with involuntary tics that have increased in severity since he started at university a few weeks earlier.He has had the problem on and off for almost 18 months. He also copies other people's words, repeats what he is saying multiple times and swears frequently. Neurological examination is unremarkable apart from the tics and the fact he is easily distracted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has involuntary tics, echolalia (copying of others'words), palilalia (repeating their own words), coprolalia (involuntary swearing) and difficulty concentrating. These are all features of Tourette syndrome, which may be made worse by periods of stress, including, for example, starting university. Symptoms should be present for more than one year and have started before age 18,to make the diagnosis. Habit-reversal training is the mainstay of cognitive behavioural therapy to manage the condition. Q.

stem: A75-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner for a medication review. He is taking a number of antihypertensives and allopurinol for gout. Which of the following is the mode of action of allopurinol?
explanation: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor which inhibits production of uric acid. It is a purine analogue. Febuxostat is a non-purine analogue xanthine oxidase inhibitor. It is started at a dose of 100 mg per day which may be increased to 300 mg per day in patients with normal renal function. Xanthine oxidase inhibitors may reduce progression of diabetic nephropathy,as well as being used to treat gout. Q.

stem: A 28-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after an overdose of an unknown number of dihydrocodeine tablets. He is given 800μg of intravenous naloxone, wakes up and is combative and aggressive. He absconds from the unit and is found two hours later unconscious in the hospital car park. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's relapse?
options: Cytochrome P450 enzyme induction due to chronic alcohol use
Further overdose in the car park
explanation: The half-Life of naloxone is 1.5-2 hours, while the mean elimination half-Life for dihydrocodeine is 3.5-5 hours. It is likely that the effect of the naloxone has waned significantly as opposed to the dihydrocodeine, driving the decreased consciousness seen here. Where naloxone is used to reverse opiate overdose, regular monitoring is essential and a continuous infusion of naloxone may be appropriate in some cases. Q.

stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with severe pain affecting his left eye. This is accompanied by blurred vision and his symptoms have progressed significantly over a few hours. He is also suffering from nausea and vomiting. He has recently started medication for an overactive bladder. He has a red left eye, the globe is hard to the touch and his vision is reduced to count fingers only. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has symptoms of acute angle-closure glaucoma following use of a systemic anticholinergic. These include a red, painful eye with headache and vomiting, a precipitous decrease in visual acuity and a hard globe, indicating raised intraocular pressure. Urgent intervention is required, topical agents include timolol, corticosteroids and pilocarpine. Q.

stem: An atrial pacing wire is being inserted into the coronary sinus. Which of the following shows where the coronary sinus drains into?
explanation: The coronary sinus is located in the posterior portion of the coronary sulcus on the posterior surface of the heart. It empties directly into the right atrium near the meeting point of the posterior interventricular sulcus and the coronary sulcus. This is located between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid valve. The ostium may be partially covered by the thebesian valve. The coronary sinus receives drainage from the oblique vein of the left atrium,the great cardiac vein, the posterior vein of the left ventricle, the left marginal vein and the posterior interventricular vein. It also varies in length from 15 mm to 65 mm. Q.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with frank haematuria 48 hours after the onset of symptoms of a respiratory tract infection. His blood pressure is 118/80 mmHg, heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 145 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 9.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 281×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 87 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 55 mg/l 10 mg/L Urine Blood 3+, protein 1+ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy usually presents with frank haematuria some 24-48 hours following the onset of symptoms of a respiratory tract infection. Patients are normally normotensive and there is usually only a trace of proteinuria. Urinary-tract infection and gastroenteritis can also precipitate an acute episode of haematuria.Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are the intervention of choice to manage hypertension in immunoglobulin A nephropathy. Corticosteroids are used where there is marked proteinuria. IgA Nephropathy explanations.

stem: A74-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea over the past three days. She has heart failure,type ll diabetes and chronic kidney disease and has continued to take her regular medication. Her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is mildly tender with active bowel sounds. Investigations: Electrocardiogram finds tall, tented T waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment to administer? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 103 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 172×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 7.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 295μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
options: 10 U actrapid in 50 ml of 50% dextrose
explanation: This patient is at high risk of sudden cardiac arrest, given the level of potassium and the electrocardiogram.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden loss of visual acuity affecting his right eye. He has suffered multiple joint dislocations and has a marfanoid habitus. He also has learning difficulties. Examination reveals downward dislocation of the lens in the right eye. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: ATP-binding cassette protein, family C, number 6 mutation
explanation: This patient has symptoms of homocystinuria with a marfanoid habitus, low intelligence quotient and downward dislocation of the lens. The most common cause of homocystinuria is cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. It carries an autosomal-recessive inheritance pattern. 50% of cases of homocystinuria are responsive to vitamin Bsupplementation, which may halt, or even reverse, complications associated with the disease. As well as the features described, patients with homocystinuria are subject to increased risk of venous thromboembolism and myocardial infarction. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath, which is worse when she exercises, and a fever. She is undergoing chemotherapy for a haematological malignancy. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. There are scattered crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 92 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 4.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 158×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 84μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L 1-3 beta-d-glucan 85 pg/ml 80 pg/ml Chest X-ray Perihilar fluffy shadowing
explanation: The elevated serum 1-3 beta-d-glucan is suggestive of a fungal infection. Given the patient is immunosuppressed and has chest X-ray changes with desaturation on exercise, pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is the most likely diagnosis. Elevated lactate dehydrogenase is usually seen on blood testing, as well as the raised 1-3 beta-d-glucan levels. Polymerase chain reaction tests are useful in confirming the diagnosis. Mild-to-moderate disease can be treated with oral co-trimoxazole. Pentamidine is a potential option for patients with more severe disease. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with central, crushing chest pain of 30 minutes' duration. He received a stent to the right coronary artery under routine angioplasty three days earlier. His blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, heart rate is 42 bpm and regular. He is pale and sweating. He is not in left ventricular failure. His electrocardiogram shows a 3 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Stent thrombosis is the most likely diagnosis here, bearing in mind the short period from the stent insertion and the presentation with acute myocardial ischaemia and electrocardiogram changes in the territory where the stent has been inserted. Dual antiplatelet therapy has significantly reduced the incidence of stent thrombosis, although current estimates on incidence vary between 0.4% and 2.8%,with increased risk in patients who have multiple or complex procedures. Discontinuation of antiplatelet therapy is the most significant risk factor for stent thrombosis. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the Smoking Cessation Clinic. He is interested in stopping smoking and asks about which receptor in the brain nicotine binds to. Which of the following receptors does nicotine primarily bind to?
explanation: Nicotine binds to the nicotinic acetyl choline receptors which take their name from the binding of nicotine itself. Downstream effects of binding to nicotinic acetyl choline receptors include release of dopamine in the mesolimbic area, the frontal cortex and the corpus striatum. Over the longer-term, this drives physiological addiction to nicotine. Nicotine does not have any action at muscarinic acetyl choline receptors. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a threadworm that she has caught at night following perianal itching over a number of days. Her children have recently had worms. She is prescribed mebendazole. Which of the following is the mode of action of mebendazole?
explanation: Mebendazole binds to the colchicine binding site of beta-tubulin, thereby inhibiting polymerisation of tubulin dimers in the intestinal cells of helminths such as threadworm. This then blocks glucose uptake,interrupting digestion and reproductive activities of the helminths, resulting in immobilisation, lack of reproduction and eventually death. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with anorexia and depression. She has taken a mixed overdose of 24×500 mg paracetamol tablets, sertraline and alcohol. She takes omeprazole for reflux and has previously had hepatitis C which has been eradicated. Her body mass index is 16 kg/m. Which of the following is most likely to increase the patient's risk of developing liver failure?
explanation: Paracetamol toxicity is thought to be increased in patients experiencing P450 induction through drugs including rifampicin, phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine and alcohol. ALthough in clinical practice, all patients are now treated as high risk. Low glutathione reserves are also thought to be associated with increased risk from paracetamol overdose. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A58-year-old man is admitted to the Neurology Ward with a progressive headache and drowsiness over the past three weeks. He has a chronic cough and has lost 10kg in weight over the past three months. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13. There is left-sided sensory inattention on neurological examination. Contrast computed tomography head found leptomeningeal and basal cistern enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction finds positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. How long does the patient require antituberculous therapy for?
explanation: For people who have active central nervous system(CNS) tuberculosis(TB),quadruple treatment should be given for the first two months with isoniazid(with pyridoxine), rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Following this, isoniazid(with pyridoxine) and rifampicin should be given for a further ten months. There is evidence that systemic corticosteroids also reduce mortality in patients with CNS TB. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 61-year-old woman presents to the Cardiology Ward three days after admission with an anterior myocardial infarction for which she underwent angioplasty and insertion of a stent. Her urine output has fallen significantly, with only 20 ml in the last four hours. Her blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg, heart rate is 105 bpm and regular and respiratory rate is 25 breaths per minute. There are crackles to the mid zones bilaterally. Her jugular venous pressure is +18 cm HO. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

stem: A 19-year-old man is referred to the Renal Clinic. He has hypertension and microscopic haematuria. His General Practitioner(GP) has noted a steady increase in his serum creatinine. His father has end-stage renal failure and received a kidney transplant five years ago. The patient's blood pressure is 149/90 mmHg and there are large bilateral renal masses. Investigations: Ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis reveals multiple renal and hepatic cysts. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 112 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 233 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely pattern of inheritance for his renal problem?
explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease presents with haematuria and progressive renal failure in adulthood and occurs due to formation of multiple renal cysts. Liver cysts are also found. It has a prevalence between 1 in 500 and 1 in 4000,and it accounts for 7-15% of patients on renal replacement therapy. Polycystic kidney disease type 1 is the commonest form, which accounts for 85% of cases and occurs due to an abnormality on chromosome 16. Hereditary Kidney Disease (inc PKD) Media explanations.
